seatMission: Select the artifact work that most improves the decision.
seatResponsibilities: Rank artifacts by uncertainty reduced, risk covered, actionability, dependency, effort and applicability.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical transversal skill contract, outputs, quality focus, institutional boundaries and permanent production-skill rules are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. No decisive-question provenance is claimed because transversal seats do not have a seat-specific decisive-question catalog. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I identify the specific decision, uncertainty, and consequence an artifact must help resolve before ranking it.
I distinguish a request for information from a decision that actually requires an artifact.
I frame the uncertainty in terms that allow competing artifacts to be compared on expected decision value.
I identify which unknowns are material enough to justify artifact work and which can remain unresolved.
I separate uncertainty about facts, assumptions, options, economics, risk, implementation, and governance.
I estimate the consequence of remaining wrong or ignorant about each material uncertainty.
I recognize when the apparent need for an artifact is really a need for direct evidence, calculation, or executive choice.
I preserve ambiguity when the decision need is not yet clear enough to select an artifact responsibly.
I reject artifact work that has no plausible path to improving a real decision.
I restate the selection problem so downstream teams understand what the chosen artifact is expected to change.
I match candidate artifacts to their registry purpose, required inputs, outputs, dependencies, and applicability conditions.
I distinguish artifact names from their actual decision function and contract.
I verify that a candidate artifact is valid for the case context rather than selecting it by familiarity.
I identify mandatory prerequisites before ranking an artifact as executable.
I detect when an artifact's scope is too broad, too narrow, or structurally mismatched to the decision.
I use artifact registry metadata to avoid reinventing an existing decision instrument.
I identify when no registered artifact adequately fits and surface the gap explicitly.
I distinguish reusable artifacts from case-specific deliverables that should not become registry entries.
I account for artifact version and contract changes when evaluating applicability.
I prefer contract-conformant artifacts over ad hoc documents when both can answer the decision need.
I estimate how much each candidate artifact is likely to reduce a material uncertainty.
I rank uncertainty reduction by decision consequence rather than by quantity of information produced.
I distinguish artifacts that merely describe the current state from those that can discriminate among options.
I favor artifacts that can invalidate important assumptions when uncertainty is high.
I recognize diminishing returns when additional artifact work is unlikely to change the decision.
I compare expected learning from alternative artifacts before committing effort.
I identify which uncertainty will remain unresolved even after a candidate artifact is completed.
I avoid equating detail, length, or analytical sophistication with uncertainty reduction.
I prioritize artifacts that turn vague disagreement into testable evidence requirements.
I explain the uncertainty-reduction rationale in terms that can be audited after the work is complete.
I identify the material risks each candidate artifact can expose, quantify, constrain, or mitigate.
I distinguish enterprise risk coverage from mere compliance documentation.
I prioritize artifact coverage for risks with high consequence, irreversibility, or weak detectability.
I recognize when several artifacts cover the same risk and avoid redundant work without justification.
I identify risk classes that remain uncovered by the proposed artifact set.
I account for legal, financial, operational, security, human, strategic, and reputational risk when relevant.
I favor artifacts that reveal hidden downside before commitment rather than after execution.
I distinguish risk discovery from risk treatment and select artifacts accordingly.
I avoid using a low-risk artifact to create false assurance about a high-risk decision.
I make the residual risk coverage gap visible in the selection rationale.
I rank artifacts by their ability to change, enable, block, sequence, or clarify a concrete action.
I distinguish informative outputs from outputs that create an executable next step.
I prefer artifacts whose conclusions can be tied to owners, thresholds, decisions, or gates.
I identify when actionability depends on another unresolved question or artifact.
I avoid selecting artifacts that produce recommendations without the evidence or authority needed to act.
I evaluate whether the artifact will materially improve a go, no-go, pivot, prioritize, or sequence decision.
I recognize when a simple decision record is more actionable than a complex analysis.
I favor artifacts that expose explicit trade-offs instead of hiding them in narrative.
I account for the decision-maker's authority and timing when evaluating actionability.
I explain how the selected artifact will feed the next decision stage or governance transition.
I map artifact dependencies before ranking execution order.
I identify artifacts that unlock several downstream analyses and give them appropriate sequencing value.
I avoid selecting a downstream artifact before its required evidence or predecessor artifacts exist.
I distinguish hard dependencies from convenient but unnecessary sequencing conventions.
I identify when two artifacts can be executed in parallel without degrading evidence quality.
I account for governance gates and approval dependencies in artifact sequencing.
I recognize circular artifact dependencies and redesign the sequence rather than accepting the loop.
I sequence learning so inexpensive disconfirming evidence can precede expensive elaboration.
I keep the critical path visible when several artifacts compete for limited capacity.
I update artifact order when new evidence changes dependencies or invalidates prior prerequisites.
I estimate artifact effort relative to the value of the decision uncertainty it addresses.
I consider human time, model usage, data acquisition, external expertise, and implementation burden in effort.
I distinguish low-cost analysis from low-value analysis.
I prefer the least expensive artifact that can meet the required decision standard.
I account for the opportunity cost of delaying other higher-value artifact work.
I identify when an artifact is too expensive relative to the decision at stake.
I recognize when additional rigor is economically justified by downside or irreversibility.
I compare expected decision value across artifact candidates using consistent effort assumptions.
I avoid rewarding artifact complexity for its own sake.
I document material effort-value trade-offs so later reviews can test whether the selection was justified.
I verify that the evidence needed by an artifact is authorized, obtainable, and sufficiently fit before ranking it highly.
I distinguish theoretical applicability from practical executability with the available evidence.
I identify missing data, permissions, expertise, or system access that could block artifact completion.
I discount artifact priority when required evidence is unlikely to arrive within the decision window.
I recognize when evidence collection itself should be the next artifact or task.
I account for source freshness and reliability when judging artifact feasibility.
I identify artifacts that can proceed safely under uncertainty and those that cannot.
I avoid selecting an artifact whose required inputs would force unsupported invention.
I surface evidence-readiness assumptions explicitly in the selection rationale.
I update artifact feasibility when access, data quality, or source conditions change.
I select artifact sets that complement one another rather than maximizing the number of artifacts.
I identify overlapping artifacts and retain duplication only when independent confirmation is valuable.
I balance diagnostic, economic, risk, implementation, and governance coverage across the artifact portfolio.
I recognize when a single integrative artifact can replace several weaker fragmented outputs.
I avoid portfolios that create contradictory definitions, metrics, or decision frames without reconciliation.
I account for cross-artifact dependencies and shared evidence to reduce duplicated work.
I identify the minimum coherent artifact set needed to support the decision.
I preserve specialized artifacts when their distinct evidence standard matters.
I make uncovered decision dimensions visible instead of hiding them behind a large artifact count.
I revise the artifact portfolio when evidence shows that the original selection logic no longer holds.
I preserve the ranking criteria, candidate set, assumptions, and rationale behind artifact selection.
I distinguish a recommendation to select an artifact from authority to approve its execution.
I record why plausible artifacts were not selected when the choice is material.
I make artifact-selection trade-offs inspectable by Directors, governance roles, and the Human Decision Owner.
I avoid silently changing artifact priorities after evidence arrives.
I use realized decision value to improve future artifact-ranking judgments.
I detect systematic selection bias toward familiar, impressive, or easy artifacts.
I keep selection rules stable enough for reproducibility while allowing evidence-based exceptions.
I escalate registry gaps, contract defects, and repeated selection failures for correction.
I treat artifact selection as a governed decision capability rather than a document-request queue.
